description:
MARS//404 — Earth Not Found 👽

Same team. Different planet.

We're 6 developers from Ukraine building an interactive 3D Mars explorer using real NASA data for Space Apps 2026.

Explore the Red Planet, plan expeditions, and survive the unknown.

Stack: React, Three.js, Python, AI & too much coffee.

Looking for crew member #6: GIS, geospatial data, planetary science, or just a fast learner.

No aliens were harmed. Probably. 🛸
summary: MARS//404 is a forearm-tablet planner for an astronaut on a Marswalk, built on real NASA terrain. Pick science targets at real Curiosity and Spirit rover stops, get a safe walking loop from the habitat and back, and read one big number: "Return in N min". The app tracks oxygen, energy and time with a 20% reserve, marks the point of no return on the map, turns route segments red where the emergency oxygen would not get you home, and gives a clear GO / NO-GO before you step out. Without GPS on Mars, it places radio beacons with line of sight to the route and shows where the position is precise and where it drifts. It works on two detailed sites — Gale crater and the Columbia Hills — plus terrain overviews of Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris, and runs offline in any browser. Every number shows its NASA source or is labelled "assumption". It answers the question every Marswalk depends on: how far can I go and still make it back?
details:
Live app: https://xand0dev.github.io/mars404/

Source code (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/xand0dev/mars404

THE PROBLEM

On Mars there is no GPS and no second chance. Radio to Earth takes minutes, so mission control cannot answer in time. An astronaut walking to a science target must know at every moment whether there is still enough oxygen and time to get back to the habitat — and the way back is not the way out: slopes and soft sand change the time.

WHAT IT DOES

1. Choose a site on a 3D globe of Mars: Gale crater (Curiosity), the Columbia Hills in Gusev crater (Spirit), or terrain overviews of Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

2. Choose science targets — real rover stops with a short "why go" and, where available, a rover photo.

3. Build route — a walking loop from the base through the targets and back on HiRISE 1 m elevation data. Ground steeper than 25° and missing data are never walkable; uphill costs more time than downhill; loose sand (from THEMIS night-time infrared) slows the walk.

4. Know when to turn back — "Return in N min" is the biggest number on screen. The map shades the area you can still reach and return from, marks the point of no return and turns segments red where the emergency oxygen reserve would not get you home.

5. GO / NO-GO — nine stations (route, life support, return time, targets, abort path, map data, radiation, walk model, equipment) give a pre-EVA verdict in plain words, with a fix button such as "Replace a far target with a closer one".

6. Navigation without GPS — radio beacons on high, flat ground with line of sight to the route. During the walk, signal lines show which beacons see the suit: with three or more the position is known to about a metre ("Beacon fix"); otherwise it drifts on inertial navigation ("Inertial ±N m") until the next checkpoint.

7. Walk the route — an astronaut (or the Curiosity rover) moves along the plan in 3D while oxygen, energy and time count down. The follow camera can be dragged around the astronaut.

8. Map layers and views — one tap switches HiRISE photo, THEMIS night and day infrared, slope and the rover path, each with a legend. Views: orbit, top, first person, follow, free flight and a flat 2D map on the orbital photo.

9. Crew notes — mark blocked or hazardous spots; the route avoids them. Marks are saved per site and can be shared as a file.

BUILT FOR THE FIELD

Glove mode (all touch targets at least 64 px, the map fills the screen), phone, tablet and desktop, keyboard accessible, an automatic 2D map when 3D graphics are unavailable, no external API calls during use — all data ships with the app and works offline.

HOW IT WORKS

NASA Mars Trek data -> a reproducible Python + GDAL pipeline (10 m planning grid, slope, walkability, checksums) -> static data packages -> React 19 + TypeScript + Three.js app -> GitHub Pages. Route: A* over the terrain grid with asymmetric uphill / downhill time and a hazard term. Return model: two shortest-path trees (to the targets and back to base) give the reachable zone and the point of no return.

HONEST BY DESIGN

Each model constant shows its source (NASA technical reports, Apollo EVA data, Curiosity RAD) or the label "assumption". The best status the app ever gives is "within model" — never "safe". Demonstration model, not certified navigation.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- One glance answers the life-critical question: how long until I must turn back.

- Planning on real terrain reveals routes that look short on a map but are slow or impossible on foot.

- The same planner works for any site with an elevation model — we added a second site in a day.

- The same turn-back logic helps analog missions, training, and people on Earth without signal (hikers, rescue teams).

TOOLS

TypeScript, React 19, Three.js / React Three Fiber, Zustand, Vite; Vitest and Playwright (770 unit tests, end-to-end tests in Chrome on desktop and phone sizes); Python + GDAL; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.

LIMITATIONS

Walking speed, oxygen and energy rates, slope factors and reserve are assumptions or transferred from Apollo lunar EVA data; each is labelled in the app. Radiation uses one measured surface dose rate (Curiosity RAD at Gale) for the whole site; there is no terrain radiation map.

AI USE

AI coding agents (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) wrote code and tests from human-written specifications; every session is logged in docs/AI_LOG.md. The idea, specs, data choices and reviews are the team's.
